function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can follow locally (or in a CI job) to get the repository ready for deployment.  
I’ve included the exact file contents that you’ll need to create/overwrite, and a short explanation of each step.  

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually run `git clone`, `git add`, `git commit` or `git push` from here, so you’ll have to execute those commands yourself on your machine (or in a CI pipeline).  

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you’re doing this in a CI job, you can skip the manual clone – the `actions/checkout` step in the workflow below will handle it.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & Create/Update Files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create or overwrite `Dockerfile` in the repo root:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – lightweight Node.js runtime
FROM node:18-alpine

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json & lockfile first – allows Docker cache reuse
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command to start the app
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

> *Why this Dockerfile?*  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small, fast, and contains the latest LTS Node.js.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees reproducible installs.  
> * The container listens on port **3000** – adjust if your app uses a different port.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can keep it in a `k8s/` sub‑folder or at the repo root – just make sure the path matches what you’ll reference later):

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        # Replace <your-registry> with your actual registry (e.g. ghcr.io/zelarhq)
        image: <your-registry>/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # Change to NodePort or ClusterIP if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # External port exposed by the service
    targetPort: 3000  # Port inside the pod
```

> **Tip** – If you’re using GitHub Container Registry (GHCR), the image name would look like `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file called `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Node.js
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      # Install dependencies
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      # Run tests (if you have a test script)
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test || true   # `|| true` keeps the job from failing if no tests exist

      # Build Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t ${{ secrets.REGISTRY }}/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }} .

      # Push Docker image to registry
      - name: Push Docker image
        env:
          REGISTRY: ${{ secrets.REGISTRY }}
          REGISTRY_USER: ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_USER }}
          REGISTRY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          echo $REGISTRY_PASSWORD | docker login $REGISTRY -u $REGISTRY_USER --password-stdin
          docker push $REGISTRY/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}

      # Optional: Deploy to Kubernetes (requires kubeconfig in secrets)
      # - name: Deploy to K8s
      #   env:
      #     KUBECONFIG_DATA: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
      #   run: |
      #     echo "$KUBECONFIG_DATA" > kubeconfig
      #     export KUBECONFIG=$(pwd)/kubeconfig
      #     kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

> **What you need to set up in GitHub Secrets**  
> * `REGISTRY` – e.g. `ghcr.io/zelarhq`  
> * `REGISTRY_USER` – your registry username (often your GitHub username for GHCR)  
> * `REGISTRY_PASSWORD` – your registry password/token  
> * (Optional) `KUBECONFIG` – base64‑encoded kubeconfig if you want the workflow to deploy automatically.

---

## 3️⃣ Add All Changed Files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you added the files in a different location, adjust the paths accordingly.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically on the `main` branch, building the Docker image and pushing it to your registry.

---

### Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Dockerfile created/updated |
| ✅ | Kubernetes deployment & service YAML created |
| ✅ | GitHub Actions workflow created |
| ✅ | Git add/commit/push performed |

---

### Troubleshooting

| Issue | Fix |
|-------|-----|
| Docker build fails because `index.js` is missing | Verify the entry point file name (`index.js` vs `app.js`) and update the Dockerfile accordingly. |
| Kubernetes deployment shows “image not found” | Ensure the image name in `deployment.yaml` matches the registry/tag you pushed to. |
| GitHub Actions fails to log in to registry | Double‑check the secrets (`REGISTRY`, `REGISTRY_USER`, `REGISTRY_PASSWORD`). For GHCR, the token must have `write:packages` scope. |

---

That’s it! Once you’ve pushed the changes, the CI pipeline will build and publish your Docker image, and you’ll have the Kubernetes manifests ready for deployment. Happy coding!
